follow_up_reason: One-week recheck after a common cold

clinician_brief.prior_note: One week ago, Emily was seen for a three-day history of sore throat, runny nose, mild cough and tiredness, thought to be a common cold. No fever or shortness of breath. She was advised to rest, drink fluids, and use over-the-counter medicine for comfort; no antibiotics were given.
active_problems: Recent upper respiratory infection (common cold), resolving
previous_plan: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Use over-the-counter medicine for symptom relief
Return if symptoms worsen or a fever develops
Follow up in about one week if not fully better
results_and_observations: No tests were needed at the first visit
today_tasks: Ask how the cold symptoms are now
Ask specifically about the leftover cough
Check for new or worsening symptoms
Address her worry about her upcoming exam

patient_private.interval_history: Sore throat and runny nose are almost gone; still has a mild dry cough, worse at night.
patient_private.adherence: Took Tylenol for the first three days, then stopped once the sore throat improved.
patient_private.treatment_response: Feels much better, has more energy, and is sleeping well again.
patient_private.new_symptoms_and_red_flags: No fever, no shortness of breath, no chest pain, no ear pain.
patient_private.agenda: Wants to know if the leftover cough is normal or needs treatment.
patient_private.concern: Worried the cough might get worse right before her exam.
patient_private.preference: Would rather not start a new medicine unless it's really necessary.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Distinguishing a normal post-viral cough tail from one that needs treatment, one week after an uncomplicated cold
clinical_knowledge.review_status: guideline-grounded sample; clinician review still recommended before release
core_concepts: A dry cough commonly lingers for two to three weeks after the other cold symptoms (sore throat, congestion) have resolved — this is expected post-viral airway irritation, not a sign the infection is still active.
By one week, the sore throat and runny nose are already 'almost gone,' which is the typical resolution timeline for a rhinovirus-type common cold and argues against a secondary bacterial process.
A cough that is worse at night but not accompanied by fever, chest pain, or breathlessness is far more likely to be residual airway hyperreactivity than pneumonia or a new problem.
Reassurance is a treatment: explaining why the cough is expected to keep improving over the next one to two weeks directly answers her practical worry about her upcoming exam.
diagnostic_clues: Sore throat and runny nose almost resolved, only a mild dry cough remains — a pattern of stepwise symptom resolution typical of a self-limited viral URI, not a new or worsening illness.
Cough worse at night is a classic feature of post-viral cough and of pooling secretions/airway irritation when lying flat, rather than a marker of severity on its own.
No fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, or ear pain rules out the main red flags that would suggest pneumonia, a secondary bacterial infection, or otitis media.
Improved energy and sleep alongside the resolving cough show the overall trajectory is toward recovery, which is more informative than any single symptom in isolation.
common_misconceptions: Worried the cough might get worse right before her exam — a reasonable fear, but a simple, non-worsening dry cough with no other symptoms is very unlikely to suddenly escalate; anticipatory guidance on the expected timeline addresses this directly.
Assuming any lingering cough after a cold means the infection never went away or needs antibiotics, when post-viral cough is a normal part of upper airway recovery, not ongoing infection.

Believing that stopping acetaminophen once the sore throat improved was 'stopping treatment early' — acetaminophen was only for comfort, so tapering it off as symptoms eased was appropriate, not a lapse in adherence.
Would rather not start a new medicine unless it's really necessary — worth honoring, since most residual post-cold cough resolves without any specific treatment beyond time and symptomatic measures.
dangerous_errors: Prescribing antibiotics for a lingering dry cough without fever or purulent signs, which does not treat a viral cough and only adds unnecessary side-effect risk.

Failing to specifically ask about fever, breathlessness, chest pain, and ear pain before reassuring her, since these are the findings that would change the picture from 'normal recovery' to 'needs further workup.'
Dismissing her stated worry about the exam without addressing it directly, which can leave her anxious enough to self-medicate or seek unnecessary care elsewhere.
Assuming resolution without checking that the cough is truly improving in frequency/severity over the week rather than just being reinterpreted as 'not so bad.'
management_principles: Confirm the trajectory (sore throat and congestion resolving, cough persisting alone) fits the expected timeline for a self-limited cold before reassuring her.
Screen explicitly for red flags — fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, ear pain — to rule out a secondary process before closing the visit.
Give a clear, honest timeline: most post-viral cough resolves within one to three weeks, which lets her plan around her exam without over-worrying.
Offer simple non-drug measures (fluids, honey if appropriate, humidified air) rather than a new prescription, matching her preference to avoid unnecessary medicine.
boundaries_and_exceptions: If the cough persists beyond three to four weeks, or a fever, wheeze, or chest pain develops, this reassurance-based plan no longer applies and further evaluation (e.g., for asthma, pertussis, or a secondary infection) is warranted.

In patients with underlying lung disease, smokers, or the immunocompromised, a lingering cough after a viral illness deserves a lower threshold for closer follow-up than in an otherwise healthy young adult.
